blocks: Snail Kite Rostrhamus sociabilis Accipitridae size and color selectivity of Apple Snail Pomacea flagellata Ampullaridae
By Alissa Genthon and Natalia Corrales

In Costa Rica's Palo Verde National Park, the specialist predator Rostrhamus sociabilis (Snail Kite) inhabits a freshwater marsh where it specifically hunts for Pomacea flagellata (Apple Snails). It is thought that the Snail Kite is selective for specific size ranges of the Apple Snail. In this study, Apple Snail size selectivity was explored by comparing sizes of prey to a representation of the available Apple Snail population in order to exploit Snail Kite bias toward size extremity within the population. Snail Kites in this study were selective for larger, more rare snails, indicating that not only does the Kite specialize in type of prey, but also in size of prey. In addition, color selectivity was observed and determined to be unrelated to selection of the snails. Finally, the study evaluated any existing snail selectivity for specific plant species to determine the complexity of the system in which the Snail Kite must hunt. Apple Snails were found to have a higher density among Bladderwort (Utricularia gibba), but this density was also shown to vary with other factors such as surface temperature, vegetative thickness, and presence of emergent vegetation. In any case, Snail density and size distribution, which are ultimately dependent on the health of the habitat, limits the success of the Snail Kite population.

Evolutionarily, specialization has become an important mechanism for the success of many species. As a specific example, the Snail Kite (Rostrhamus sociabilis Accipitridae) has an almost exclusive predator-prey relationship with the Apple Snail³,⁴,⁵ (Pomacea flagellata Ampullariidae). Snail Kites are more common in freshwater marshes and sloughs, and their population ranges from southern Florida and southeastern Mexico to Ecuador and northern Argentina.⁷ In Costa Rica, they are found in the Tempisque basin and Rio Frio-Cano but are rare in the lowlands of these regions.⁷ Seasonal movement is normal for Snail Kites as they must respond to changing water levels from wet to dry seasonal variations, which affects availability of prey.⁷ The Snail Kite depends primarily on the Apple Snail that inhabits tropical and neotropical freshwaters and consumes local aquatic plants or floating vegetation.⁵

Although the Apple Snail is consumed by several predators (crocodiles, turtles, fish, other bird species, and young alligators), each specialist predator has a separate foraging method which clearly distinguishes their distinct niches.⁵ The Snail Kite, a medium sized raptor, utilizes two different foraging techniques to capture its prey: the course-hunting technique and still-hunting technique.³ In the first, the Snail Kite will fly low over the marsh using its visual acuity to locate snails up to 16 centimeters below the marsh surface.⁴ It then carries its prey to a designated perch and uses its curved beak to remove the operculum of the snail, permitting the Kite full access to the snail meat.³ With the second technique, the Snail Kite will remain at its perch until it locates a snail. The prey in each case is carried back to a specific perch where it is consumed, and the shell is then discarded into a pile below the perch. According to Collett (1977), although Apple Snails reach a range of sizes during a lifetime, Snail Kites normally consume snails of a “large” size because they hunt by sight. Also, Snyder and Kale (1983) attribute the failure of Snail Kites to consume smaller snails to the fact that extraction is more difficult with a smaller snail, as there is a smaller opening to remove the operculum. It has also been shown by Bourne (1985) that Snail Kites forage in order to maximize caloric return per energy expenditure which would imply a tendency toward snails of larger size.

Both the predator and the prey in this situation depend on the presence of emergent vegetation for survival. Apple Snails are found in freshwater marshes, lakes, rivers, and springs, which all must include emergent vegetation in order to provide breathing and egg laying surfaces. Apple Snails also depend on the aquatic plants within the marsh habitat as a food source.⁵ The Snail Kite also requires emergent vegetation or perches in order to successfully locate and consume its prey. In effect, there is a certain degree of association between wetland plants and the Snail Kite-Apple Snail relationship. Because of this, the health of the wetland habitat becomes a limiting factor to the success of the Snail Kite. This has recently become an important issue since the Snail Kite is now endangered in Costa Rica (Wildlife Conservation Law 7317).
